processing: A preparation, not a leaf style: tea is made on an open fire with dried herbs such as thyme or sage, often with spices such as cardamom or cinnamon.
harvest_season: Not applicable as a seasonal tea; it depends on the tea and dried herbs at hand.
appearance_dry: A mix of dark tea leaf and grey-green dried herbs, sometimes with whole spices.
appearance_wet: Dark tea leaf mixed with softened herbs and spices.
taste_profile: Strong tea with the savoury lift of thyme or sage, and warmth when cardamom or cinnamon goes in.

brewing.notes: A home approximation: simmer tea and herbs in one pot, then strain. Amounts vary by household and there is no fixed recipe.

vintage_note: It has no vintages and is made fresh on the spot. Packaged mixes sold under the name are ordinary blends, so read the ingredients and buy for fresh-smelling herbs.
description:
Bedouin tea is less a kind of leaf than a habit: black tea boiled on an open fire, sweetened hard and usually scented with a dried herb. In Jordan it is the tea a guide brews on the trail or a host pours in a desert camp.

Water, sugar and leaf go into the kettle together and stay on the heat until the liquor turns deep amber. Boiling pulls out far more tannin than steeping would, and the heavy sugar is what keeps that in balance.

Expect something sweet, strong and herbal, with sage or thyme most prominent in Jordan. Cardamom or cinnamon also turn up, so the name covers a loose family and not one recipe.

At home, use loose leaf rather than bags, go lightly with the sage since it quickly turns medicinal, and sweeten to taste. Small glasses suit it better than a mug.
history: Little is documented about when this preparation took its present form. It is described as a practice of nomadic Bedouin within the wider Arabic tea tradition, and it has no known inventor or dated origin.
